title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Supervisory Intervention** (Vol IV). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

Most deployed robots keep a person in reserve for the situations their learned policies cannot handle, and that reserve is usually treated as the final safeguard. A person, however, needs a large fraction of a second to respond even while watching closely and several seconds after only monitoring. A machine moving at walking pace covers meters in that time, so a request for help can consume the very clearance the help was meant to protect.

nodes.label: Human Authority, Reaction Time, and Clea

rows: **Intervention transfers the right to propose**

Supervisory intervention transfers the right to propose on named actuator channels from the policy to an authenticated person, committed on a control tick and bounded by a lease, while every human command still passes the permission check.
**Takeover delay in the stopping budget**
Takeover latency (sensory, cognitive, motor, console) is long-tailed and must be budgeted at a design percentile as a delay before braking, which sets the speed a supervised machine may run.
**Clearance-derived fallback deadline**

Fixing the current speed and solving the stopping inequality for the wait gives the latest fallback deadline, so a handover timeout is a function of state, and any configured ceiling is clipped to it.
**Authority leases and physical presence**

Autonomous chunks and manual sessions hold separate leases on the safety MCU's clock, so a silent policy, a dropped link, or an incapacitated operator loses authority to a state-matched local fallback.
**Single-writer handover handshake**
Per channel, authority resolves every tick to exactly one state with the enforcer the sole actuator writer, and a four-phase request-acknowledge-commit-release handshake moves it.
**Bumpless transfer**

A setpoint swap at commit demands an unbounded command derivative, so the enforcer blends between latched endpoints with a quintic smoothstep whose duration is set by the rate limit and paid from stopping reserve.
**Mode confusion and per-channel annunciation**
Single-writer gating resolves arbitration faults but not mode confusion, the gap between the mode a supervisor believes and the actual one, which only per-channel masks and annunciation fix.
**Authority record**

The authority record binds a sealed static authority manifest to a per-tick evidence tuple of time, authority state, measured state, proposed and admitted commands, so every handover is reconstructable and attributable.
**Authenticating interventions**
Protective stops never wait for verification while motion commands, which inject energy, must be authenticated, attributable, and fresh, and the verifier's availability must itself be protected.
**Causal intervention masking**
A takeover log is split into intervals by commit, blend-end, and stabilization timestamps, and only the stabilized human interval trains as demonstration.
**Trustworthy operational logs**
Reconstruction needs a log that survives physical failure and records both sides of the causal boundary on synchronized clocks, because dispatched commands alone cannot prove delivered torque.
**Ironies of automation**
Automation leaves the human the hardest, least-time cases with degraded skill and a stale forward model, so oversight degrades exactly when it is needed.
**Shared autonomy blending**
Blending human and policy commands works only when goals are unimodal and every intermediate blend is admissible; across modes a convex combination is a new, unchecked command.
**Remote-assistance session admission**
A remote assistant is admitted only if reaction budget, handshake latency, manual lease, and blend window fit the remaining clearance, and remote assistance is never a safety layer.
